# Introducing Dynamic Dreaming in Supermemory — supermemory

Dreaming is magical.

> TL;DR
> 
> We're launching Dynamic Dreaming in supermemory today, which automatically works if you're using supermemory in any way - API, OpenClaw, Hermes agent, etc.

We (humans) dream to condense and reflect on our thoughts, not only things that happened today, but a weird blend of everything that has ever happened. It's how we connect dots that don't have obvious wires between them.

A conversation you had three weeks ago clicks with something you read this morning, and you wake up with an idea that wasn't there the night before.

Most memory systems don't do this. They learn instantly, the moment data flows in, and then never look at it again. A fact gets written and it just sits there - a frozen snapshot of one moment, oblivious to everything that has shifted around it since.

Some systems take a smarter swing at this. Claude Code, for example, condenses its context when the window fills up, summarizing what's been said and packing it down. Better, but still a single pass. Whatever the summarizer thought mattered at that one moment is what gets kept. Everything else is gone.

We think both of these approaches have their own caveats - What if the conversation was only half done when you learnt something? Or what if the user asks about the last conversation in this one?

A user spends twenty minutes debating two architectures and lands on option B in the very last message, but the system already wrote down "prefers option A" from the middle of the discussion. Every future session is now quietly poisoned. Or what about the user who comes back tomorrow and asks about _yesterday's_ conversation, only to find that the only thing left of it is a three-line summary that decided, prematurely and forever, what mattered?

### Dynamic Dreaming

Memory shouldn't be a transcript. It shouldn't be a snapshot.

It DEFINITELY shouldn't be a hash table you write once and read forever (like other memory providers). It should _think about what it knows_, on its own, in the background, and get better at remembering you the longer it lives.

So we built dynamic dreaming.

Best part? If you're already a user of supermemory, **this will just work.** Use it in your OpenClaw, or Hermes Agent. Just ask your agents to use supermemory. No additional configuration is required on your end. You'll be able to see a "Dreaming" symbol next to memories that will be dreamt on.

### It just works

When you go quiet, or when enough new context has piled up, Supermemory will now enter a dream cycle on its own.

No cron job, no fixed timer. The system decides when, and it decides how deep to go based on what the heuristics tell it. A quick reflection for a short session. A longer dive when the day's worth of context warrants it.

During a dream, Supermemory does what brains do at night. It reconsolidates what it already knows. It merges fragments that belong together. It generates new abstractions over the raw material.

And the part that matters most: it reweights old facts in light of everything that's come in since they were written.  
Memories that were too confident get tempered.  
Memories that contradicted each other get resolved.  
Memories that were just sitting there, isolated, suddenly find their neighbors.

The output isn't a summary.  
It's three things at once: new memories, a graph of _inferences_ (we also call them derivations) that weave between them, and a weighted, evolving picture of who the user actually is. Not a static profile, but a thought-out view that updates as the evidence changes.

![Supermemory chat suggestion card titled "From Mumbai to CEO" asking how self-taught origins shaped problem-solving](https://supermemory.ai/_astro/image-1.Byvzb6NH_12j68P.webp)

The card above is a real inference. None of those facts were written together. The Mumbai jailbreak, the O1 visa, the two acquisitions, the GitHub stars. They came in over months, across dozens of separate conversations, in no particular order. Dreaming is what stitched them into a single thought. The narrative emerged on its own.

This is the thing we're most excited about: dynamic dreaming connects dots that, frankly, we thought were uncatchable.

**It is the closest thing I've seen to a context window that never expires.**

### Still real-time

This part took us the longest to get right. If dreaming takes time, what happens when a user asks about the conversation that just ended thirty seconds ago, before any dream has touched it?

Nothing breaks. Supermemory's hybrid retrieval keeps unprocessed content queryable the moment it arrives, falling back to conversation search for memories that haven't been dreamt yet. New context is available instantly. The dreamt state catches up in the background, at most fifteen minutes, and when it does, the agent gets a richer version of the same truth.

And every inference stays grounded. We don't let the system invent things it can't trace back to source memories. If it can't show its work, it doesn't get to claim the thought.

### What changes

Agents stop forgetting the things that matter. Contradictions get caught and reconciled instead of silently rotting in the index. User profiles stop being a brittle list of attributes and start being something closer to understanding. And the longer you use Supermemory, the better it gets. Not because it's accumulating more data, but because it's actually _thinking about_ the data it has.

We've been building memory infrastructure for a year. This is the first feature that makes memory feel less like a database and more like a mind.

Dream away.

Use supermemory today. [supermemory.ai](https://supermemory.ai/)

## Applying this in an application

When moving beyond a local prototype, use the [connector ingestion guide](https://supermemory.ai/blog/agent-memory-ingestion-connectors/) to test synchronization and permissions. Define [correction, retention, and deletion behavior](https://supermemory.ai/blog/memory-lifecycle-retention-corrections-deletion/) for imported documents and derived context.

Keep [source connectors separate from memory policy](https://supermemory.ai/blog/connector-provider-separation/) and test [whether remembered context improves the user outcome](https://supermemory.ai/blog/useful-agent-memory-acceptance-tests/). For research workflows, preserve [an evidence ledger](https://supermemory.ai/blog/research-agent-evidence-ledger/) so derived conclusions remain traceable.

jsonLd.headline: Introducing @supermemory/tools v2.0.0
jsonLd.description: supermemory/tools v2.0.0 unifies the API across agent SDKs from AI SDK to Mastra, makes conversation identity first-class, and turns on memory by default.

mainEntity.name: What is new in @supermemory/tools v2.0.0?

acceptedAnswer.text: This release unifies the API across all agents sdk integrations from AI SDK to Mastra, makes conversation identity a first-class concept, and ships with memory saving on by default. Key changes include: Unified config-object API, customId as a required conversation identity, memory saving on by default, and VoltAgent verbose and profile-mode warnings fixed.

mainEntity.name: What is the Unified config-object API in v2.0.0?

acceptedAnswer.text: In v1.x, each integration had a slightly different call signature. In v2.0.0, every integration shares the same options object. One API. Four integrations. Same mental model everywhere — covering Vercel AI SDK, OpenAI SDK, Mastra, and VoltAgent.

mainEntity.name: Why is customId now required in v2.0.0?

acceptedAnswer.text: In v1.x, conversationId (or threadId in Mastra) was optional. When omitted, conversations weren't grouped — each turn was saved in isolation, making it impossible to retrieve the full context of a session later. In v2.0.0, customId is required across all integrations. Omitting it or passing an empty string throws at construction time, so you catch the error immediately rather than silently losing conversation context in production.

mainEntity.name: What changed about memory saving defaults in v2.0.0?

acceptedAnswer.text: In v1.x, addMemory defaulted to 'never'. Memory saving had to be explicitly enabled, which meant it was easy to forget — and easy to deploy an agent that retrieved memories but never built any new ones. In v2.0.0, addMemory defaults to 'always'. When a conversation ends, it's automatically saved to Supermemory and becomes available for retrieval in future sessions. No extra configuration required.

mainEntity.name: What are the three memory retrieval modes available?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three modes control what gets retrieved before each LLM call: 'profile' — retrieves the user profile built from past sessions; 'query' — semantic search across past memories based on the current message; 'full' — both profile and query results combined (highest recall).

mainEntity.name: How do I migrate from v1.4.x to v2.0.0?

acceptedAnswer.text: The changes in v2.0.0 are mechanical. For Vercel AI SDK, OpenAI, and Mastra users: 1) Move containerTag from the positional argument into the options object, 2) Rename conversationId or threadId to customId, 3) Add addMemory: 'never' if you relied on the old default. For VoltAgent users, no API changes are required. Most teams are done in under 5 minutes.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between containerTag and customId in @supermemory/tools v2.0.0?

acceptedAnswer.text: containerTag scopes memory to a user, workspace, or tenant — it answers 'who does this memory belong to.' customId identifies which conversation a turn belongs to, grouping all messages from a session into one retrievable document. For example, containerTag might be 'user-123' while customId is 'chat-2026-04-26' or a session UUID.

mainEntity.name: Can I use @supermemory/tools in a browser environment without process.env access?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Pass your API key directly via the apiKey option in the config object instead of relying on process.env.SUPERMEMORY_API_KEY, and the package works in browser and other non-Node environments. This was added between v1.0 and v2.0 specifically to support edge and browser runtimes.

mainEntity.name: What happens to my LLM call if Supermemory is unreachable during memory retrieval?

acceptedAnswer.text: By default, skipMemoryOnError is true, so the LLM call proceeds with the original prompt if memory retrieval fails. Set skipMemoryOnError: false if you want the call to fail hard instead. An internal fetch timeout also ensures retrieval never hangs your response indefinitely.

mainEntity.name: Which memory retrieval mode should I use for a real-time chat app vs. a batch personalization pipeline?

acceptedAnswer.text: For real-time chat where you want the highest recall, use mode: 'full' — it combines the user profile and semantic search results. For lighter personalization where you only need stable preferences, mode: 'profile' is cheaper since it skips the search query entirely. Use mode: 'query' when semantic search against past sessions matters more than the static user profile.

mainEntity.name: Does @supermemory/tools v2.0.0 support the Mastra agent framework?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Import SupermemoryInputProcessor and createSupermemoryOutputProcessor from @supermemory/tools/mastra. Both accept the same unified config-object shape as the Vercel AI SDK and OpenAI integrations, and RequestContext support lets you pass per-request thread IDs.

mainEntity.name: How do I control how retrieved memories are formatted before they're injected into my system prompt?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pass a promptTemplate function in the config object. It receives a MemoryPromptData object that exposes userMemories, generalSearchMemories, and raw searchResults, so you can wrap memories in custom XML tags, filter by metadata, or restructure the injection format entirely before it reaches the model.

mainEntity.name: What performance optimizations does @supermemory/tools v2.0.0 include to reduce token waste and latency?

acceptedAnswer.text: The package ships with memory deduplication (duplicate memories are removed before injection), an LRU cache for repeated lookups within a session, multi-step prompt caching for Vercel AI SDK multi-turn flows, and parallel execution of Claude memory tool calls instead of sequential processing.

mainEntity.name: What is the fastest way to add persistent memory to an existing OpenAI SDK integration?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wrap your OpenAI client with withSupermemory from @supermemory/tools/openai, pass a containerTag and customId in the config object, and memory saving is on by default — no other config required. Install with npm install @supermemory/tools@^2.0.0 and get an API key at console.supermemory.ai.

mainEntity.name: How does @supermemory/tools v2.0.0 handle conversation grouping differently from v1.x?

acceptedAnswer.text: In v1.x, the conversation ID field was optional and named differently per integration (conversationId in Vercel/OpenAI, threadId in Mastra), so turns were often saved in isolation with no way to retrieve a full session later. In v2.0.0, customId is required across all integrations and throws at construction time if omitted or empty, catching the misconfiguration before it silently loses production context.

mainEntity.name: When should I set addMemory: 'never' in @supermemory/tools v2.0.0?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use addMemory: 'never' when you want retrieval without writing new memories — common in read-only contexts, test environments, or evaluation runs where you don't want test conversations polluting the memory store. The default in v2.0.0 is 'always', so opt-out must be explicit.

# @supermemory/tools v2.0.0 Is Here — supermemory

Today we're releasing v2.0.0. This release unifies the API across all agents sdk integrations from AI SDK to Mastra, makes conversation identity a first-class concept, and ships with memory saving on by default.

**What's new in v2.0.0:**

*   Unified config-object API
*   customId: required conversation identity
*   Memory saving on by default
*   VoltAgent: verbose and profile-mode warnings fixed
*   Everything that shipped from v1.0 to v2.0

> **Upgrading from 1.4.x?** The changes are mechanical — most teams are done in under 5 minutes. See the [v1.4 → v2.0 migration guide](https://supermemory.ai/docs/migration/tools-v2-upgrade).

## Unified config-object API

In v1.x, each integration had a slightly different call signature. Vercel AI SDK and OpenAI took `containerTag` as a positional argument. Mastra used constructor arguments in a different order. Every integration had its own name for the conversation ID field — `conversationId` in Vercel and OpenAI, `threadId` in Mastra.

This made the package harder to learn and harder to switch between integrations. If you built on Vercel AI SDK and wanted to add a Mastra processor, you had a different API to memorize.

In v2.0.0, every integration shares the same options object:

```
import { withSupermemory } from "@supermemory/tools/ai-sdk"
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai"

const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "conv-456",
  mode: "full",
  addMemory: "always",
})
```

The same shape works on OpenAI:

```
import { withSupermemory } from "@supermemory/tools/openai"

const client = withSupermemory(new OpenAI(), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "conv-456",
})
```

And on Mastra:

```
import { SupermemoryInputProcessor } from "@supermemory/tools/mastra"

const input = new SupermemoryInputProcessor({
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "conv-456",
  mode: "full",
})
```

One API. Four integrations. Same mental model everywhere.

> Note
> 
> **for VoltAgent users:** VoltAgent already used a config-object signature before v2.0.0, so your call shape is unchanged. See the VoltAgent section for what actually changed in your integration.

To learn more, see the [integration documentation](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/ai-sdk).

## customId: required conversation identity

In v1.x, `conversationId` (or `threadId` in Mastra) was optional. When omitted, conversations weren't grouped — each turn was saved in isolation, making it impossible to retrieve the full context of a session later.

In v2.0.0, `customId` is required across all integrations. Omitting it or passing an empty string throws at construction time, so you catch the error immediately rather than silently losing conversation context in production.

```
// This throws immediately with a clear error message
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "",  // ❌ throws: customId must be a non-empty string
})
```

```
// Use a stable, meaningful ID — a session UUID, thread ID, or date-scoped key
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: `chat-${sessionId}`,  // ✅
})
```

`customId` groups every message from a session into a single conversation document in Supermemory, making that full context available for retrieval in future sessions.

**`containerTag`** **vs** **`customId`** **at a glance:**

`containerTag`

`customId`

Represents

Who the memory belongs to

Which conversation this turn belongs to

Scope

User, workspace, or tenant

Session, thread, or conversation

Example

`"user-123"`, `"acme-corp"`

`"chat-2026-04-26"`, a UUID

Memory search

Scoped to this tag

Groups messages into one document

To learn more, see the [Vercel AI SDK integration](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/ai-sdk) or the [migration guide](https://supermemory.ai/docs/migration/tools-v2-upgrade).

## Memory saving on by default

In v1.x, `addMemory` defaulted to `"never"`. Memory saving had to be explicitly enabled, which meant it was easy to forget — and easy to deploy an agent that retrieved memories but never built any new ones.

In v2.0.0, `addMemory` defaults to `"always"`. When a conversation ends, it's automatically saved to Supermemory and becomes available for retrieval in future sessions. No extra configuration required.

```
// v1.x — had to opt in
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), "user-123", {
  addMemory: "always",  // easy to forget
})

// v2.0.0 — saves by default
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "conv-456",
  // addMemory: "always" is the default
})
```

If you want to retrieve memories without saving new ones — for example in a read-only context or during testing — opt out explicitly:

```
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "conv-456",
  addMemory: "never",
})
```

> Note
> 
> This default applies to Vercel AI SDK, OpenAI SDK, and Mastra. VoltAgent already defaulted to `"always"` in v1.x.

## VoltAgent: verbose and profile-mode warnings

VoltAgent's call shape was already a config object before v2.0.0, so there are no breaking API changes for VoltAgent users.

**Profile-mode warnings for ignored search params.** When `mode: "profile"` is set, parameters like `threshold`, `limit`, `rerank`, `rewriteQuery`, and `searchMode` have no effect — profile mode fetches the full user profile and doesn't run a search query. Previously these were silently ignored. Now a runtime warning is logged when any of them are set alongside `mode: "profile"`, so configuration mistakes surface immediately.

To learn more, see the [VoltAgent integration](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/voltagent).

## Everything that shipped from v1.0 to v2.0

v2.0.0 is a milestone, but a lot of capability landed across the releases between the initial Vercel AI SDK-only release and today.

### New integrations

`@supermemory/tools` started with Vercel AI SDK support only. Between v1.0 and v2.0, three more integrations were added:

*   **OpenAI SDK** — `withSupermemory` wrapper for `chat.completions.create`, with support for the Responses API (`responses.create`) and automatic assistant response capture
*   **Mastra** — `SupermemoryInputProcessor` and `createSupermemoryOutputProcessor` with `RequestContext` support for per-request thread IDs
*   **VoltAgent** — `withSupermemory` agent config wrapper that hooks into `onPrepareMessages` (retrieval) and `onEnd` (saving) lifecycle events

### Memory retrieval modes

Three modes control what gets retrieved before each LLM call:

```
// "profile" — retrieves the user profile built from past sessions
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), { containerTag: "user-123", customId: "conv-1", mode: "profile" })

// "query" — semantic search across past memories based on the current message
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), { containerTag: "user-123", customId: "conv-1", mode: "query" })

// "full" — both profile and query results combined (highest recall)
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), { containerTag: "user-123", customId: "conv-1", mode: "full" })
```

### Custom prompt templates

The `promptTemplate` option lets you control exactly how retrieved memories are formatted before they're injected into the system prompt:

```
import { withSupermemory, type MemoryPromptData } from "@supermemory/tools/ai-sdk"

const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "conv-456",
  mode: "full",
  promptTemplate: (data: MemoryPromptData) => `
<memory>
  <profile>${data.userMemories}</profile>
  <context>${data.generalSearchMemories}</context>
</memory>
  `.trim(),
})
```

The `data` object also exposes raw `searchResults` so you can filter by metadata before injection.

### Resilience: skipMemoryOnError and fetch timeout

Memory retrieval should never block your LLM call. Two additions make this reliable:

*   **`skipMemoryOnError: true`** (default) — if Supermemory is unreachable or returns an error, the LLM call proceeds with the original prompt. Use `verbose: true` to log when this happens.
*   **Internal fetch timeout** — memory retrieval is bounded. It never hangs your response indefinitely.

```
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "conv-456",
  skipMemoryOnError: false,  // fail the call if memory retrieval fails
})
```

### Browser and other environments support

`apiKey` can now be passed via options instead of relying on `process.env.SUPERMEMORY_API_KEY`, enabling `@supermemory/tools` to work in browser environments (and others):

```
const model = withSupermemory(openai("gpt-4o"), {
  containerTag: "user-123",
  customId: "conv-456",
  apiKey: "sm-...",  // no process.env required
})
```

### Performance improvements

*   **Memory deduplication** — duplicate memories are removed before injection, reducing token waste
*   **LRU cache** — repeated memory lookups within the same session are served from cache
*   **Multi-step prompt caching** — compatible with Vercel AI SDK's multi-turn agent flows
*   **Concurrent tool calls** — Claude memory tools execute in parallel instead of sequentially

## Migrating from 1.4.x

The changes in v2.0.0 are mechanical. For Vercel AI SDK, OpenAI, and Mastra users:

1.  Move `containerTag` from the positional argument into the options object
2.  Rename `conversationId` or `threadId` to `customId`
3.  Add `addMemory: "never"` if you relied on the old default

For VoltAgent users, no API changes are required — only review the `verbose` behavior if relevant.

```
npm install @supermemory/tools@^2.0.0
```

For before/after code for all four integrations, see the [full migration guide](https://supermemory.ai/docs/migration/tools-v2-upgrade).

For a version-pinned implementation and a two-session test, follow [persistent memory with AI SDK](https://supermemory.ai/blog/how-to-use-supermemory-with-ai-sdk/). Before a multi-user rollout, check [tenant and user isolation](https://supermemory.ai/blog/multi-tenant-memory-noisy-neighbor-isolation/).

## Get started

**Start using @supermemory/tools v2.0.0:**

*   Install: `npm install @supermemory/tools@^2.0.0`
*   Get an API key at [console.supermemory.ai](https://console.supermemory.ai/)

**Pick your integration:**

*   [Vercel AI SDK](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/ai-sdk)
*   [OpenAI SDK](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/openai)
*   [Mastra](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/mastra)
*   [VoltAgent](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/voltagent)

**Resources:**

*   [v1.4 → v2.0 migration guide](https://supermemory.ai/docs/migration/tools-v2-upgrade)
*   [@supermemory/tools on npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@supermemory/tools)
*   [GitHub](https://github.com/supermemoryai/supermemory)

For an existing application, start with [a reversible memory rollout](https://supermemory.ai/blog/add-memory-to-existing-app-rollout/). For coding workflows, compare [filesystem memory design](https://supermemory.ai/blog/filesystem-memory-design/) with the integration boundary your agent uses.

mainEntity.name: What is the fundamental problem with semantic search?

acceptedAnswer.text: Semantic search fundamentally struggles with precision. Because it's just matching vector proximity, there's often noise in those top results. Just because a document uses similar words doesn't mean it actually has the context to answer the user's question.

mainEntity.name: What is the problem with re-ranking as a solution to search precision?

acceptedAnswer.text: Re-ranking is fantastic for precision. It guarantees that the documents returned are highly relevant. But it suffers from a massive flaw: Recall. You are still constrained by your search limit. If your limit is set to 3, but answering the user's question completely requires pulling context from 5 different documents, you are stuck. You simply do not have enough 'slots' to fit the complete answer into the context window.

mainEntity.name: What is Supermemory's Aggregation feature and how does it work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Aggregation looks at the same corpus of data, and respects the exact same result limit. However, instead of one slot equalling one literal document, each result slot is a synthesis of multiple documents condensed into one. By condensing multiple relevant memories to take up only one search result space, you no longer have to choose between precision and recall. You get both.

mainEntity.name: Why is Aggregation especially powerful for multi-session LLM use cases?

acceptedAnswer.text: This feature is incredibly powerful for multi-session use cases. It allows developers to maintain a very small search limit—keeping downstream LLM token usage low, less reasoning effort, and latencies lightning fast—while still achieving the ridiculously high recall and precision required to answer complex questions.

mainEntity.name: How do you enable Aggregation in the Supermemory API?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can simply turn on aggregate: true in the Supermemory API to get started.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between semantic search and memory in AI systems?

acceptedAnswer.text: Semantic search retrieves documents by vector proximity — it finds text that looks similar to your query but has no notion of state, contradiction, or time. Memory, by contrast, tracks relationships between pieces of knowledge, handles updates and contradictions, and evolves as the user interacts — giving your AI a persistent understanding rather than a one-shot lookup.

mainEntity.name: How does search result aggregation differ from re-ranking?

acceptedAnswer.text: Re-ranking adds a reasoning step to select the most relevant documents from your top-K results, which improves precision but leaves recall capped at your search limit. Aggregation instead synthesizes multiple documents into each result slot, so a limit of 2 can still surface context drawn from 5 or more underlying memories — you get both precision and recall without raising your limit.

mainEntity.name: What happens to token usage and latency when you use aggregation instead of raising your top-K limit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Aggregation keeps your search limit small, which directly reduces the tokens passed to your downstream LLM and the reasoning effort required — both lower cost and faster response times. Instead of feeding the LLM 20 raw documents hoping it finds the answer, you feed it 2 or 3 dense, pre-synthesized results that already contain the relevant context.

mainEntity.name: What is the precision-recall tradeoff in search, and why is it hard to solve?

acceptedAnswer.text: Precision measures how relevant the returned results are; recall measures how much of the relevant information you actually retrieve. Raising your top-K limit improves recall but floods the LLM with noise, hurting precision. Lowering the limit sharpens precision but misses context, hurting recall. The two goals pull in opposite directions, and standard keyword or vector search offers no way to satisfy both at once within a fixed result budget.

mainEntity.name: Can I control how many aggregated results are returned, or is the output format fixed?

acceptedAnswer.text: The aggregation feature respects whatever result limit you already set in your query — passing aggregate: true does not change the number of slots returned. Each slot simply becomes a synthesis of multiple underlying memories rather than a single raw document, so you keep full control over the size of the context passed to your LLM.

mainEntity.name: Should I use aggregation for simple single-turn queries or only for complex multi-part questions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Aggregation delivers the most obvious value for complex, multi-part, or multi-session queries where a single document cannot fully answer the question — like 'What is this company and who runs it?' For straightforward single-fact lookups, standard search already performs well, and aggregation adds a synthesis step that may not be worth the overhead for that simpler case.

mainEntity.name: How does Supermemory's memory graph handle contradictions or updated information compared to a flat vector store?

acceptedAnswer.text: A flat vector store indexes embeddings and returns whatever is most similar to your query — it has no mechanism to recognize that two documents conflict or that one piece of information supersedes another. Supermemory's memory graph tracks ontology-aware edges, handles knowledge updates and merges, and understands temporal ordering, so when a user's preference or fact changes, the graph reflects that update rather than returning stale context alongside current context.

mainEntity.name: How do I build a memory layer for my AI app without assembling five separate services?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supermemory ships retrieval, memory, user profiles, connectors, and extractors as composable primitives in a single API — you can adopt one building block or wire together the full stack. The setup takes under 10 lines of code and integrates with LangChain, Vercel AI SDK, CrewAI, and other frameworks you're likely already using, so you're not ripping out your existing infrastructure.

mainEntity.name: What is SuperRAG and how does it handle retrieval differently from a standard vector search index?

acceptedAnswer.text: SuperRAG is Supermemory's retrieval primitive — it runs hybrid vector and keyword search, applies context-aware reranking, and supports advanced metadata filtering and per-user scoping, all at sub-300ms latency. Unlike a plain vector index that returns the closest embeddings, SuperRAG integrates with the memory graph so retrieved documents carry relationship and temporal context, not just similarity scores.

mainEntity.name: What makes multi-session recall particularly difficult for standard RAG pipelines?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard RAG pipelines retrieve from a static document store with no awareness of what was asked across previous sessions, who the user is, or how their context has changed over time. When a query requires synthesizing signals from multiple past interactions — as most real-world personalized applications do — a fixed top-K retrieval window simply cannot hold enough slots to reconstruct the full picture, which is exactly the gap that aggregation and a persistent memory graph are built to close.

text:
Solving the Precision-Recall Tradeoff in Search — supermemory
When you're building memory for AI, search is your foundational layer. The way search generally works is straightforward: the user defines a query, and then sets a limit (top-K) on how many search results they want returned. Usually, this is set to 10 or 20.
Once the request hits the server, a response is returned sorted by semantic similarity. More often than not, this basic semantic match answers the query decently well.
However, there's a catch.
Semantic search fundamentally struggles with precision. Because it's just matching vector proximity, there's often noise in those top results. Just because a document uses similar words doesn't mean it actually has the context to answer the user's question.
The Problem with Re-ranking
To solve this precision issue, the industry introduced re-ranking. What re-ranking does is add a reasoning step—usually through a cross-encoder model or an LLM—to pass over the retrieved data and select what would actually be the best match to the query.
Re-ranking is fantastic for precision. It guarantees that the documents returned are highly relevant. But it suffers from a massive flaw: Recall.
You are still constrained by your search limit. If your limit is set to 3, but answering the user's question completely requires pulling context from 5 different documents, you are stuck. You simply do not have enough "slots" to fit the complete answer into the context window.
And if you're using an LLM anyways, might as well do the entire reasoning and only give the LLM what it needs.
The Supermemory Approach: Aggregation
We built Aggregation to solve exactly this issue.

# Solving the Precision-Recall Tradeoff in Search — supermemory

When you're building memory for AI, search is your foundational layer. The way search generally works is straightforward: the user defines a query, and then sets a limit (top-K) on how many search results they want returned. Usually, this is set to 10 or 20.

Once the request hits the server, a response is returned sorted by semantic similarity. More often than not, this basic semantic match answers the query decently well.

However, there's a catch.

Semantic search fundamentally struggles with precision. Because it's just matching vector proximity, there's often noise in those top results. Just because a document uses similar words doesn't mean it actually has the context to answer the user's question.

### The Problem with Re-ranking

To solve this precision issue, the industry introduced re-ranking. What re-ranking does is add a reasoning step—usually through a cross-encoder model or an LLM—to pass over the retrieved data and select what would _actually_ be the best match to the query.

Re-ranking is fantastic for precision. It guarantees that the documents returned are highly relevant. But it suffers from a massive flaw: **Recall.**

You are still constrained by your search limit. If your limit is set to 3, but answering the user's question completely requires pulling context from 5 different documents, you are stuck. You simply do not have enough "slots" to fit the complete answer into the context window.

And if you're using an LLM anyways, might as well do the entire reasoning and _only_ give the LLM what it needs.

### The Supermemory Approach: Aggregation

We built **Aggregation** to solve exactly this issue.

What aggregation does is look at the same corpus of data, and it respects the exact same result limit. However, instead of one slot equalling one literal document, **each result slot is a synthesis of multiple documents condensed into one.**

By condensing multiple relevant memories to take up only one search result space, you no longer have to choose between precision and recall. You get both.

### Seeing it in Action

Let's look at how this actually works within Supermemory. Imagine a memory space containing a bunch of unstructured data about our team and what we do.

![Memory graph of hexagonal nodes linked to documents, with a version popup showing v1 memory entries and navigation](https://supermemory.ai/_astro/image-1.D2ME0ueA_Z1uWNcF.webp)

We want to ask a complex, multi-session query: _"What is Supermemory and who is behind it?"_

To illustrate the point, we'll set our search limit to just 2.

**Without Aggregation:** When we run this standard search, it returns two memories. These memories might match part of the question fairly well, but there just aren't enough slots to completely answer both parts of the question. The limit of 2 bottlenecks the recall, leaving the LLM with an incomplete picture.

```
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
id: RbqTQjS85K88weNqZbAPzu
memory: Dhravya is the founder and CEO of Supermemory
similarity: 0.77
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
id: yHcHoGPpacSsMYxiKH4bdP
memory: Soham, Prasanna, Sreeram, and Tejas are part of the research team at Supermemory
similarity: 0.75
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

**With Aggregation:** Now, we turn aggregate to true and run the exact same query with the same limit of 2.

It still returns exactly two results—but these results are aggregated from _multiple_ underlying memories.

```
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
id: aggregated_0_1775529845474
memory: Supermemory is an AI startup positioned as the context layer for the agentic era, founded by its CEO, Dhravya.
similarity: 1.00
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
id: aggregated_1_1775529845474
memory: The team behind Supermemory includes members across various functions: the research team consists of Soham, Prasanna, Sreeram, and Tejas; Mahesh serves as an engineer, and Shardul is part of the growth team.
similarity: 0.90
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

1.  **Result 1** perfectly synthesizes multiple documents to answer the _"What is Supermemory?"_ part of the query.
2.  **Result 2** aggregates entirely different memories to completely answer the _"Who is behind it?"_ part.

### Why this matters for your LLM apps

This feature is incredibly powerful for multi-session use cases. It allows developers to maintain a very small search limit—keeping downstream LLM token usage low, less reasoning effort, and latencies lightning fast—while still achieving the ridiculously high recall and precision required to answer complex questions.

You can simply turn on

```
aggregate: true
```

In the supermemory API to get started.

It's a huge step forward in building a memory engine that actually scales with human complexity.

If you want better memory for your LLMs and apps, you can use this today. Check out our docs, and get an API key on our dashboard.

## Applying this in an application

To interpret retrieval and answer scores separately, read [what LongMemEval tests](https://supermemory.ai/blog/longmemeval-benchmark-what-it-tests/). If a real answer misses evidence, use the [memory debugging guide](https://supermemory.ai/blog/debugging-agent-memory-retrieval-postmortem/) to locate the failed stage before tuning retrieval.

Choose [vector search, graph traversal, or both](https://supermemory.ai/blog/vector-graph-hybrid-query-choice/) according to the question before comparing ranking results.

mainEntity.name: What is the main problem with OpenClaw's memory system?

acceptedAnswer.text: OpenClaw's memory system is highly reliant on tools, meaning the main agent must utilize tools for any memory operation. When you tell OpenClaw your name, it has to spend tokens and time to save it using a tool. When you ask a basic question, it needs to use the memory tool to collect context to answer. This approach is slow and counterintuitively uses MORE tokens because the tool calls are expensive. It also does not handle knowledge updates, temporal reasoning, or multi-session context well, and it does not forget irrelevant information.

mainEntity.name: How does Supermemory fix OpenClaw's memory problems?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supermemory is built with a vector-graph layer that automatically learns and updates knowledge about users. It uses HOOKS instead of tools, so saves happen implicitly in the background with both memories extracted and raw chunks saved. Every fact is built on top of other facts and is always contextual. The memory system also forgets - irrelevant information over a long time horizon will automatically decay and be forgotten, unlike static markdown files.

mainEntity.name: What are the benchmark results comparing Supermemory to other memory systems?

acceptedAnswer.text: Testing on the Memory Bench platform showed Supermemory consistently scored 10-20% better across the board. Filesystem (Claude code's memory) scored 54.2%, RAG (OpenClaw's memory) scored 58.3%, while Supermemory achieved 85.9%. The Supermemory plugin also saves on tokens used by the LLM provider, making it better, faster AND cheaper.

mainEntity.name: Why does OpenClaw's memory use tools instead of hooks?

acceptedAnswer.text: OpenClaw uses a two-layer storage system with daily append-only logs and curated long-term facts. It relies on memory_search for semantic search and memory_get to read specific lines. Because it is highly reliant on tools, the agent must use tools for any memory operation - to save information or retrieve context. Context is only fetched when needed, but this uses MORE tokens because tool calls are expensive.

mainEntity.name: What is the two-layer storage system in OpenClaw's memory?

acceptedAnswer.text: OpenClaw has memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md which are daily append-only logs that the agent reads at session start (today and yesterday), functioning as a scratchpad for running context. It also has MEMORY.md for curated long-term facts, preferences, and decisions, which is only loaded in private/DM sessions and never in group chats for privacy reasons.

acceptedAnswer.text: The Supermemory plugin provides premium memory for all your services for just $20 per month. You can set it up by visiting https://github.com/supermemoryai/openclaw-supermemory or ask openclaw to set it up for you.

# Why It Forgets + How to Fix It — supermemory

TLDR: Today, we are releasing a new version of our openclaw plugin - [github.com/supermemoryai/openclaw-super…](https://github.com/supermemoryai/openclaw-supermemory).

This post is going to be a bit technical, so bear with me (or bookmark for later!)

In this post, I will talk about what we do about OpenClaw memory, and how we fix it.

BENCHMARKS AT THE END!!! :)  

It's been about two weeks since [@OpenClaw](https://x.com/@OpenClaw) absolutely took over the internet. Everyone's been talking about it - the things it can do, how it can connect to all our tools, and how we can chat with it on our preferred messaging platform. This always-running, always working assistant.  

It's biggest problem? Memory. It's not just me saying it. We launched our plugin a [few weeks ago](https://x.com/DhravyaShah/status/2016308406701981731?s=20) (it got 500k views!!), and it is much-loved!  
just do an x search about openclaw memory. no one has good things to say about it :([x.com/pedrodias/status/2023013765911122…](https://x.com/pedrodias/status/2023013765911122065?s=20) [x.com/DhravyaShah/status/20232589583711…](https://x.com/DhravyaShah/status/2023258958371119131?s=20)

Openclaw obviously saw this - and they even added the QMD memory plugin. This should fix it, right???? ....Even today morning, I woke up to this post by [@Levelsio](https://x.com/@Levelsio) - and I did my usual plug, talking about the [@supermemory](https://x.com/@supermemory) plug etc. etc.

And, to my surprise, MANY recommended supermemory. But why? What do we do differently that the built-in version does not? How is it different from filesystem? or QMD? How does it compare on the benchmarks?I kept getting these questions - so here's a practical, technical explanation of what supermemory does differently.

## OpenClaw's memory problems

To understand this well, we first need to learn exactly how openclaw remembers things. It has a **Two-layer storage:**

![Tool-based memory flow: the agent explicitly calls MEMORY\_SEARCH and a hybrid BM25/vector pipeline returns snippets](https://supermemory.ai/_astro/image-1.Dzmt0ahh_Z1nvaUR.webp)

1.  **memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md** — daily append-only logs. The agent reads today + yesterday at session start. Think of it as a scratchpad for running context.
2.  **[MEMORY.md](https://memory.md/)** — curated long-term facts, preferences, decisions. Only loaded in private/DM sessions (never group chats, for privacy).

**Two tools (read-side):**

*   memory\_search — semantic search over all memory files. Returns snippets with file path, line range, and score. Mandatory before answering anything about prior work, decisions, dates, people, preferences. \*\*
*   memory\_get — read specific lines from a file after finding them via search.

**The problem?**

1.  It uses tools, not hooks.
    
    Because it is highly reliant on tools, you are always expecting the main agent to UTILIZE the tools to do any memory operation.  
    You tell OpenClaw your name? It has to spend tokens and time to save it, using a tool.
    
    You ask it a basic question? you have to ask it to use the memory tool to actually collect the context to answer the question.
    
    This approach is rather slow, but also context is only fetched when you need it. \*_The problem? Counterintuitively, this uses MORE, not LESS tokens - because the tool call etc are expensive too!_
    
2.  It does not handle knowledge updates, temporal reasoning, multi-session context well.
    
    When saving new things to memory, it has no idea of what's already in there (Unless you explicitly ask it to traverse through the whole memory again). This leads to it being a bit stupid when adding things, as it will add redundant information, not "update" existing knowledge, and generally not build on top of everything it knows about you.
    
3.  **It does not forget.** Forgetfulness is more important than you think. This is the primary way to keep the context fresh and useful, even after time has passed.

We have been building the context infrastructure for agent memory for years now. Throughout this time, we have learnt and built something that we think is ideal for the age of OpenClaw.

What's different? Supermemory is built with a vector-graph layer, which automatically learns and updates it's knowledge about users.

It comes with Knowledge updates, temporal reasoning, and other things. Every fact is built on top of other facts, and it's always contextual.

For the plugin, we make use of HOOKS. The saves happen implicitly, in the background, with both the memories extracted out of it, as well as the raw chunks being saved.

This is mainly because we don't know what to "remember" on ingestion time - so if something was not remembered, the chunk referencing it will show up to provide context. But it will always be there.

Importantly, this memory system also forgets! Irrelevant information over a long time horizon will automatically decay and be forgotten, unlike static markdown files.

![Hook-based memory flow: pre-request recall injects context and a post-response hook stores facts asynchronously](https://supermemory.ai/_astro/image-2.Dd229zL2_Z21wOVG.webp)

claude helped me with a nice UI to put this in picture

## Ok so the architecture is better. but benchmarks?

To verify our claims, we ran supermemory against both - OpenClaw's memory system as well as Claude code's memory system, on our open source memory evaluation platform, Memory Bench. [github.com/supermemoryai/memorybench](https://github.com/supermemoryai/memorybench)Supermemory consistently scored 10-20% better across the board.

*   Filesystem (Claude code's memory): 54.2%
*   RAG (OpenClaw's memory): 58.3% \*Note that this is expecting that the memory tool is actually called.
*   Supermemory: 85.9% \*Automatic, implicit!

The supermemory plugin also saves on tokens used (by the LLM provider), so it ends up being **better, faster AND cheaper.**

**Yeah. that's right.**

You can use it today.

Just go here or ask openclaw to set it up for you. Premium memory for all your services, for just $20 /month - [github.com/supermemoryai/openclaw-super…](https://github.com/supermemoryai/openclaw-supermemory)

# Molt Bot's Memory with Supermemory — supermemory

I'm the founder of supermemory. Clawd/Molt bot is blowing up right now, with many, many use cases. I set it up, too, and have been using it through telegram.

> TL;DR
> 
> just go to [supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/clawdb…](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/clawdbot) to set up supermemory for your clawd bot.

However, me and some other friends of mine noticed that it's memory is really bad. It almost feels like... it _never_ wants to utilize it's memory to answer questions.

![Chat where a user asks Clawd to check its memory and Clawd replies "You're right. My bad — it was literally in my memory."](https://supermemory.ai/_astro/image-1.DSLtevln_AnbeW.webp)

For such a big and successful project, this sucks. but why? We instantly got to work... [@manthanguptaa](https://x.com/@manthanguptaa) did an awesome job breaking down their architecture - [x.com/manthanguptaa/status/201578064677…](https://x.com/manthanguptaa/status/2015780646770323543?s=42) and from that, we know that it heavily relies on _tools_ to reference memory.

**The problem with tools - The models aren't trained to use them all the time.**

![iMessage thread discussing why Clawdbot's memory tool calling is unreliable and abstracting tools behind an LSP](https://supermemory.ai/_astro/image-2.B9R8pyJM_Z1dUMUY.webp)

Memory needs to be something that the model can access any time, it should just be fed into the model on every run. However, the current architecture of Molt won't work at all because of this poor memory.

## The fix.

We integrated clawd bot with supermemory - with:

*   Automatic recall at all time
*   Tools to manually search, forget, get profile, etc.
*   /remember and /recall commands

So now, you \_always\_ know that your clawd bot will have perfect memory.  

Now, i can have extremely long conversations with Molt, switch from telegram to whatsapp to slack, and it has all the context about me, synced with supermemory.This feels magical. You should try it.

If you want to learn more about supermemory, just read this - [supermemory.ai/blog/ais-next-big-thing-…](https://supermemory.ai/blog/ais-next-big-thing-personalization-and-super-memory/)

To install supermemory for your clawd bot, go here [supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/clawdb…](https://supermemory.ai/docs/integrations/clawdbot)

mainEntity.name: What is memorybench and why was it created?

acceptedAnswer.text: memorybench is an open source evaluation framework for context systems across any benchmark. It was created because developers were building internal benchmarking rigs and duplicating effort while comparing incompatible results. memorybench provides a standard way to run and compare multiple memory providers, with a Web UI, CLI, checkpoints, and batteries included.

mainEntity.name: What new connectors did Supermemory launch during Launch Week?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supermemory launched three new connectors: GitHub for syncing with files and documentation, S3 for syncing with all buckets in an S3 system, and Web Crawler for keeping websites indexed for instant answers. These connectors sit alongside existing integrations with Notion, Google Drive, and OneDrive.

mainEntity.name: How does the conversations endpoint reduce costs?

acceptedAnswer.text: The conversations endpoint processes only new tokens while keeping full context, instead of billing for every token processed like most LLM providers. This results in lower cost, more consistent conversations, and fewer moments where the AI forgets previous context.

mainEntity.name: What is hybrid search and how does it improve context quality?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hybrid search blends memory and retrieval approaches to improve context quality by 10-15 percent with a single toggle. It requires no migrations or rewrites and provides better answers by combining the strengths of both memory and RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) approaches.

mainEntity.name: What is the Supermemory Startup Program and what does it offer?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Supermemory Startup Program offers $1,000 in credits, dedicated guidance from the Supermemory team, simple setup, and six months to build and iterate. It's designed to support the next wave of builders by removing memory as a bottleneck, helping founders move from idea to working product faster.

# Supermemory's Unforgettable Launch Week — supermemory

Over the last year, one belief has guided almost everything we’ve built at Supermemory

> AI becomes meaningfully useful only when it remembers.

Memory shouldn’t be something developers rebuild from scratch.  
It shouldn’t be fragile, expensive, or trapped inside a single tool.

So during Unforgettable Launch Week, we focused on one goal -

**Make memory simpler, faster, more accessible and available wherever AI lives.**

And instead of announcing ideas, we shipped things you can use today.

Below is a recap of what went live, and why it matters.

## memorybench - a standard way to evaluate AI memory

We kept building internal benchmarking rigs. So did our users.  
Everyone was duplicating effort, and still comparing incompatible results.

memorybench changes that.

GitHub: [github.com/supermemoryai/memorybench](https://github.com/supermemoryai/memorybench)

## New connectors: GitHub, S3, and Web Crawler

Your context doesn’t live in one place. Neither does Supermemory.

These sit alongside Notion, Google Drive, and OneDrive, which many of you already rely on.

Context shouldn’t be siloed. Now it isn’t.

Docs: [supermemory.ai/docs/connectors/overview](https://supermemory.ai/docs/connectors/overview) Access in console:[console.supermemory.ai/login](https://console.supermemory.ai/login)

## Conversations endpoint - cheaper, smarter conversations

Most LLM providers bill you for every token processed, even when nothing new is happening.

Our conversations endpoint now processes only the new tokens while keeping full context.

That means:

*   lower cost
*   more consistent conversations
*   fewer “I forgot” moments

Docs: [supermemory.ai/docs](https://supermemory.ai/docs)

## Hybrid Search - where memory meets retrieval

Memory alone isn’t always enough. Retrieval alone isn’t either.

Hybrid Search blends the two, improving context quality by 10–15 percent with a single toggle. No migrations or rewrites required, just better answers.

Learn more: [supermemory.ai/docs/search/examples/mem…](https://supermemory.ai/docs/search/examples/memory-search#hybrid-search-mode)

## Stateful coding agents (opencode plugin)

Traditional coding agents degrade over time. As threads grow, they forget earlier context and repeat themselves.

The Supermemory opencode plugin makes agents stateful. They learn in real time, maintain project awareness, and adapt across sessions.

For our own team, this changed the way we build software.

GitHub: [github.com/supermemoryai/opencode-super…](https://github.com/supermemoryai/opencode-supermemory)

## Embeddable Memory Graph

People like seeing how their knowledge connects.

We made the Supermemory graph embeddable so developers can include that same interactive visualization inside their own products. One component, fully customizable, integrated directly into the user experience.

Docs: [supermemory.ai/docs/memory-graph/overvi…](https://supermemory.ai/docs/memory-graph/overview)

## code-chunk - chunking built for code

Most text splitters weren’t designed for code. They break logic, functions, and structure — which leads to poor recall.

code-chunk is AST-aware and splits at the right boundaries. In our evaluation, that improved recall by 28 points.

Docs: [supermemory.ai/blog/building-code-chunk…](https://supermemory.ai/blog/building-code-chunk-ast-aware-code-chunking/) GitHub: [github.com/supermemoryai/code-chunk](https://github.com/supermemoryai/code-chunk)

## MCP 4 - memory that travels with you

We believe users should control their memory, not platforms.

MCP 4 allows Supermemory context to work across tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Windsurf, and others, using an open Model Context Protocol server.

No lock-in. Memory that moves with you.

## The Supermemory Startup Program

We’ve benefited from communities and programs that supported us early. Now we want to extend that same support to the next wave of builders.

The Supermemory Startup Program offers:

*   $1,000 in credits
*   dedicated guidance from our team
*   simple setup
*   six months to build and iterate

We’ve already seen founders move from idea to working product dramatically faster once memory stops being the bottleneck.

Apply: [binary.so/eQvzzEk](https://binary.so/eQvzzEk) Read our blog: [supermemory.ai/blog/empowering-the-next…](https://supermemory.ai/blog/empowering-the-next-generation-of-founders-supermemory-startup-program/)

## Nova - our consumer app returns

We are bringing our VIRAL consumer app back! Say hello to NOVA.

A personal memory companion designed to help individuals organize, recall, and make sense of their knowledge across tools.

Join the waitlist: [supermemory.ai/consumer](https://supermemory.ai/consumer)

## Where we’re headed

Every launch in Unforgettable Launch Week was built around these principle

> Memory should be reliable.  
> It should be accessible.  
> And it should exist everywhere AI operates.

Whether you’re experimenting, scaling, or building something entirely new, our goal is to give you memory infrastructure that stays out of the way - while quietly powering everything beneath it.

Thanks for being part of this journey. There is a lot more coming.

# Introducing the Supermemory Startup Program — supermemory

If there’s one thing we’ve learned while building Supermemory, it’s that most startups don’t fail because they didn't build features; they fail when infrastructure slows them down, or they built too slow.

Modern AI teams are forced to solve the same problem again and again:  
how to make their products remember context reliably, affordably, and at scale.

We’ve lived that journey ourselves, and along the way, we were supported by founders, friends from the community, mentors, and early customers who believed in us and helped us stay focused on the mission.

Today, we’re proud to give back to the community that built us.

Our startup program is designed for early-stage founders who want to ship real products quickly, without rebuilding memory infrastructure from scratch.

### What you get:

*   3 months of our Scale plan, free (100% off, with ~$600/mo of usage included)
*   dedicated assistance from our team
*   fast onboarding and simple setup
*   3 months to build, iterate, and launch

We're starting this initiative with a simple goal of removing “memory complexity” as a blocker, so founders can focus on building products people love.

We’ve already seen early teams ship in days instead of months because Supermemory handled context, recall, and persistence for them. This program makes that acceleration available to anyone starting outcreating that same momentum for the next generation of builders.

### Why are we doing this?

*   Great ideas shouldn’t be gated behind infrastructure costs or months of engineering lift
*   We believe founders should be able to test ideas quickly
*   AI products should remember without any hacks
*   Teams shouldn’t have to maintain custom memory systems forever
*   And we know what a difference it makes when someone supports at the right moment

The Startup Program is our contribution to that future where founders build tools that truly understand users, grow with them, and don’t forget.

If you’re an early-stage company or about to become one, we’d love to support you.

[Apply to the program](https://binary.so/eQvzzEk) and tell us about your startup. We’ll review quickly and help you get started!

We can’t wait to see what you build.

jsonLd.name: Supermemory's Context Cloud Makes AI Infra Insanely Cheap

mainEntity.name: What is the Context Cloud?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Context Cloud marks the transition of Supermemory from just a memory system to a full context infrastructure. It offers composable 'lego blocks' including Memory, SuperRAG, Search and Traversal, and Operations — the building blocks to build agents the way they should be, with the best, most reliable, and delightful infrastructure components.

mainEntity.name: What can Supermemory do today?

acceptedAnswer.text: Today, Supermemory can: Parse and extract any modality of content (PDFs, images, etc.); Learn in real time about entities and create a growing graph about them (SOTA Memory); Large scale RAG (with a bunch of features in it); Creating profiles of your users for short-term understanding (User Profiles); Figuring out what your users are doing / understanding patterns and use cases (Qualitative Observability); Keep external services like Google Drive, Notion, S3, Crawled websites, etc. in sync in real-time (Sync); and more.

mainEntity.name: Why didn't Supermemory change its pricing before?

acceptedAnswer.text: The only thing stopping us from going all into this non-opinionated legos-for-context-infrastructure was the fact that our pricing only had two metrics attached to it: tokens ingested and search queries. Well, in reality it was just one metric (tokens) as we knew no one would hit our extremely high limit of search queries, ever.

mainEntity.name: How does the new pricing model work?

acceptedAnswer.text: In the new pricing: (1) Rich tokens / normal tokens — multi-modal content will be billed 2x normal token count; (2) Separate pricing for retrieval (which also makes it the cheapest managed retrieval service!); (3) Charging for operations — for all the little configuration that you can do with Supermemory; (4) Supermemory tokens — unlike LLM tokens, we only count and bill on the unique tokens we've seen, which means if it's an ongoing conversation with an LLM, we will literally only bill on the unique tokens in the entire conversation. Often times this is 5–10x less than text tokens themselves.

mainEntity.name: Will customers end up paying more or less under the new pricing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Depending on how you count it, this makes Supermemory the cheapest memory layer on the market. Yes, headline prices didn't move. The math underneath did. Most of you will pay less for the same workload starting next month, and some of you will pay significantly less.

mainEntity.name: What problem was Supermemory originally solving, and how did it evolve?

acceptedAnswer.text: When I first started building Supermemory, I had one goal: to build the best memory system for AI. I would talk to customers, and find out that memory was not the only thing they needed — they were all setting up 7–8 different vendors at the same time. The product kept changing and evolving, and we started doing more and more things with the product, ultimately expanding into a full context infrastructure platform.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between 'rich tokens' and 'normal tokens' in Supermemory's Context Cloud pricing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rich tokens are charged at 2x the normal token rate and apply to multi-modal content like PDFs, images, and audio. Normal tokens cover standard text. The key saving comes from how Supermemory counts tokens at all: only unique tokens across an entire conversation are billed, not every repeated token, which typically means you pay for 5–10x fewer tokens than a raw text-token count would suggest.

mainEntity.name: Should I self-host Supermemory or use the managed cloud service?

acceptedAnswer.text: Self-hosting via Docker is available across all tiers with full feature parity to the cloud, so the decision is purely about your compliance and infrastructure preferences, not capability trade-offs. Teams with strict data-residency or on-prem requirements should self-host; teams that want to ship fast without managing infrastructure should default to the managed cloud.

mainEntity.name: How does Supermemory's memory graph differ from what a vector database gives you?

acceptedAnswer.text: A vector database stores embeddings and retrieves by similarity score — it has no concept of relationships, contradictions, or time. Supermemory's memory graph tracks ontology-aware edges between memories, handles knowledge updates and contradictions, supports temporal reasoning, and can traverse multi-hop relationships — capabilities that flat vector storage cannot replicate by design.

mainEntity.name: Can I bring my own vector store instead of using Supermemory's default storage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Supermemory supports pluggable vector store backends, so you can wire in Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, or a custom store instead of the default. This means you keep your existing vector infrastructure investment and satisfy any compliance or performance requirements without duplicating data.

mainEntity.name: What is 'dynamic dreaming' and when should I use instant processing instead?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dynamic dreaming (the default) groups related documents together during ingestion to form memory from coherent semantic units, optimizing for cost and quality. Instant processing (dreaming: 'instant') handles each document in isolation for immediate recall at the cost of one additional operation per document. Use instant processing for real-time chat and personalization; use dynamic dreaming for batch ingestion pipelines and periodic syncs.

mainEntity.name: How does Supermemory handle audio and multi-modal content ingestion?

acceptedAnswer.text: Audio files — voice recordings, podcasts, and meeting recordings — are automatically transcribed via Gemini 2.5 Flash, then chunked and indexed into the memory graph with no third-party transcription service required. PDFs, images, web pages, PowerPoint files, and video are also supported natively through the Extractors primitive, all included free on every plan.

mainEntity.name: What frameworks and agent SDKs does Supermemory work with?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supermemory has official SDKs for TypeScript and Python, plus framework integrations for Vercel AI SDK, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI SDK, Mastra, Pipecat, and Microsoft Agent Framework. It also ships an MCP server, a CLI, and plugins for Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, OpenClaw, and Windsurf — so it slots into whichever toolchain you are already using.

mainEntity.name: How does Supermemory's retrieval latency compare to Mem0?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supermemory delivers sub-300ms recall. Mem0 retrieval runs at 7–8 seconds. That gap matters in production: multi-second retrieval stalls the agent's response loop in ways users feel immediately, while sub-300ms retrieval keeps the interaction feeling responsive.

mainEntity.name: What compliance certifications does Supermemory hold, and can it run inside a VPC?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supermemory holds SOC 2 Type 2, HIPAA, GDPR, and CASA certifications, with encryption in transit and at rest plus fine-grained access controls. VPC deployment is available at the Enterprise tier, and full self-hosting via Docker is available across all tiers for teams that need data to stay within their own infrastructure boundary.

mainEntity.name: What's the fastest way to get Supermemory running in an existing agent project?

acceptedAnswer.text: Run 'npx supermemory' for a five-minute setup, or use 'npx supermemory install-plugin' to automatically detect your environment and install all supported plugins in a single step. For framework integration, install via 'npm i supermemory' and connect through whichever SDK your agent already uses — Vercel AI SDK, LangChain, and Mastra all have native integrations.

*   Parse and extract any modality of content **(PDFs, images, etc.)**
*   Learn in real time about entities and create a growing graph about them (**SOTA Memory**)
*   Large scale **RAG** (with a bunch of features in it)  
    (And RAG+Memory available as a filesystem [smfs.ai](https://smfs.ai/))
*   Creating profiles of your users for short-term understanding (**User Profiles**)
*   Figuring out what your users are doing / understanding patterns and use cases (**Qualitative Observability**)
*   Keep external services like **Google Drive, Notion, S3, Crawled websites, etc. in sync in real-time (Sync)**
*   ... and more.

All of these have been natural progressions of how we think agents will be built - with lego blocks, or composition of multiple such layers, using them in the best way possible to get things done.

Each use case of memory is slightly different, and has different tradeoffs. A healthcare assistant needs to remember things about health, but also needs best quality retrieval, with a latency tradeoff being acceptable. Similarly, a research/coding assistant using subagents might be OK to load things into context in the explore phase.

To serve all of these use cases, we started opening up our API and stopped being opinionated. So now, supermemory is truly _yours._ It's your legos to build whatever you can wish.

Me and the team sat together to find what can \_not\_ be built with supermemory, and honestly, we could not come up with any good answer.

### Why we did not change the pricing before

The only thing stopping us from going all into this non-opinionated legos-for-context-infrastructure was the fact that our pricing only had two metrics attached to it: \`tokens ingested\` and \`search queries\`

Well, in reality it was just one metric (tokens) as we knew no one would hit our extremely high limit of search queries, ever.

So, we started deciding the new pricing: It had to be composable yet easy - Unit-based but not credits, as we don't want people to worry about credits and wonder how our pricing works (We wanted to give our users full transparency)

In our new pricing, we figured it out - All usage draws from the same credit pool, and is very clear on what is offered.

1.  Rich tokens / normal tokens - Multi-modal content will be billed 2x normal token count
2.  Separate pricing for retrieval (Which also makes it the cheapest managed retrieval service!)
3.  Charging for operations - For all the little configuration that you can do with supermemory, they are now counted as operations.
4.  Supermemory tokens - Unlike LLM tokens, we only count and bill on the unique tokens we've seen. Which means if it's an ongoing converastion with an LLM, we will literally only bill on the unique tokens in the entire conversation. Often times this is 5-10x less than text tokens themselves.

![Supermemory pricing cards: Memory $0.005, SuperRAG $0.001, Search and Traversal $0.005, Operations $0.10 per 1K](https://supermemory.ai/_astro/image-1.BCYw5g1y_Z15jSSq.webp)

Depending on how you count it, this makes Supermemory the cheapest memory layer on the market. yes, headline prices didn't move. The math underneath did. Most of you will pay less for the same workload starting next month, and some of you will pay _significantly_ less.

And now, no matter what, our customers have the perfect breakdown of how much they spend.

![Daily spend bar chart with a tooltip showing 184.2K rich memory tokens, 33.6K text tokens, 86 operations and 479 queries](https://supermemory.ai/_astro/image-2.C3kPObKa_PsTp8.webp)

This, along with the launch of our filesystem ([smfs.ai](https://smfs.ai/)) marks the transition of supermemory moving from just a memory system to becoming the Context Cloud.

The legos to build your agents, the way they should be. And we provide the best, most reliable, and delightful infrastructure components that doesn't break your bank while helps you build and ship fast.

We're ready for the next chapter. are you?

# Supermemory Raises $3M to Build AI Memory — supermemory

Today, I am excited to announce our first funding round to accelerate our mission of building an **interoperable, scalable and reliable memory for LLMs and agents**.

Memory is one of the hardest challenges in AI right now. We have really intelligent models (Claude, GPT-5, etc) and tools (Cursor, and many others), and I genuinely believe that the next hard frontier will be personalization. And that's the problem we're solving at supermemory - self-learning context about your users that is interoperable any model.

It all started as a consumer app built over the summer last year - to help _humans_ organize the knowledge they collect on various apps. At the time, Supermemory was not trying to be a business. It was an open-source "second brain" app that users loved. We quickly reached 50k+ users, millions of items saved by these users, and [10,000 stars on Github](https://git.new/memory), and it was one of the _**fastest growing OSS projects**_ in 2024. Very quickly, this side-project turned into a real business.  

At scale, the consumer app ran into many issues - and to our surprise the infrastructure for "Memory" for LLMs like this simply didn't exist. I had some experience in infrastructure and started sharing more details on how we were building the infrastructure behind the consumer app ourselves.  

At the time, I was working on AI [infrastructure at Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/embedded-function-calling/), where we filed a patent to make agents faster. I worked at startups working on memory, made multiple consumer-led apps, and much more. Doing this, I realized the real problems with memory - it's not just a search problem, it's about really understanding the users and making their experience magical by contextualizing the LLMs they talk to.

While many loved the consumer app, and the project won the [buildspace grant](https://buildspace.so/), among many others, a lot of interest came from companies wanting this infrastructure for their products. Many were ready to pay right away, and many offered contractual or consultancy work for help with setting up the open-source project, and that's when we decided to open up the _infrastructure_ for everyone to use.

We built our own [vector database](https://x.com/DhravyaShah/status/1853637539053113758), [content parser](https://github.com/supermemoryai/markdowner) and extractor, and a lot of infrastructure components were built from scratch, purpose-driven for being a flexible, scalable memory layer that works like the [human brain](https://supermemory.ai/blog/memory-engine/).  
After all this work, Supermemory managed to top every benchmark and extremely scalable while _providing some of the best latencies in the market._

Today, we have the best, scalable and fastest memory engine.

Ever since then, our customers have been loving supermemory in every way. Today, some send us many _**billions of tokens every week,**_ and our product is loved by enterprise customers like Cluely, Composio etc. as well as open source projects like Scira AI.

Today, I am excited to announce the next chapter of supermemory - We have raised $3 million dollars led by [Susa Ventures](https://www.susaventures.com/) (Shaheer), Browder Capital, SF1.vc, with participation from top angels like Dane Knecht (CTO Cloudflare), Theo Browne, David Cramer, Julian Weisser at [Solo founders program](https://www.solo.club/), and others leading in the space of infrastructure and AI.

We are hiring across engineering, research and product roles. Join us in the journey of creating the best memory engine on 🌎

mainEntity.name: What is the main problem with text splitters for code chunking?

acceptedAnswer.text: Text splitters split code at arbitrary character limits without understanding code structure. When you split Python at 500 characters, you end up cutting functions in half. The embedding for this chunk has no idea what the code does. Text splitters don't understand code structure, so if someone searches for relevant code, they might get useless fragments.

mainEntity.name: How does code-chunk differ from traditional text-based chunking approaches?

acceptedAnswer.text: code-chunk uses tree-sitter to parse source code into an AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) and uses the tree structure to find natural split points like functions, classes, and methods. It chunks at semantic boundaries instead of arbitrary character limits. The library extracts semantic entities including signatures, documentation comments, parent relationships, and import sources.

mainEntity.name: What is contextualized text and why does it matter for embeddings?

acceptedAnswer.text: Each chunk includes a contextualizedText field that prepends semantic context to the raw code, including file path, scope chain, entity signatures, imports used, and sibling context. Embedding models are trained on natural language, so when you embed code without context, the model doesn't know relationships. By prepending this context, the embedding captures semantic relationships that pure code misses.

mainEntity.name: What performance improvements does code-chunk show in benchmarks?

acceptedAnswer.text: After fixing the benchmark with hard negatives and IoU thresholds, code-chunk achieved 70.1% Recall@5 and 0.43 IoU@5, compared to chonkie-code at 49.0% Recall@5 and 0.38 IoU@5, and fixed-size baseline at 42.4% Recall@5 and 0.34 IoU@5. In agent-based eval on SWE-bench Lite, semantic search reduced duration from 2.0m to 1.2m, tokens from 4.3k to 2.4k, and cost from $0.25 to $0.20.

mainEntity.name: What languages does code-chunk support and how do I use it?

acceptedAnswer.text: code-chunk supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, Go, and Java. Basic usage: import { chunk } from 'code-chunk', then call const chunks = await chunk('src/user.ts', sourceCode). For RAG, use contextualizedText when generating embeddings. The library also supports streaming for large files, batch processing with controlled concurrency, and works in WASM environments like Cloudflare Workers.
